The two possibilities make opposite predictions about the role of knowledge, and that single divergence adjudicates between them. It does *not*, we stress at the outset, identify *why* sophistication amplifies. Three accounts survive the test, against which only the information-deficit and naïve-Bayesian readings fall: motivated reasoning (capacity recruited to defend identity), divergent information environments (the engaged of each side absorbing more of their own diet, §5), and expressive responding (the sophisticated being better at knowing and *reciting* their side's line). What follows establishes the comparative static — that the gap grows with sophistication, not shrinks — and reads it as consistent with asymmetric motivated reasoning, while narrowing but not eliminating the other two; the section title claims only what the evidence licenses, that the capture is *not an information deficit*.

## Emergence among the educated (GSS)

In the GSS, the partisan gap on the fact emerges *first* among the college-educated. By 2014 it stood at roughly twenty-one points among graduates while remaining near zero among non-graduates, diffusing to the rest of the electorate only later (@fig-mechanism). Sorting that appears first where the capacity to evaluate evidence is highest is the signature of motivated reasoning, and it mirrors the elite-to-public diffusion of the precedence result — capture begins at the top, in both the elite-mass and the sophisticated-unsophisticated sense. We report this as a temporal ordering rather than a single coefficient, because across so few survey-years the pooled interaction is positive but imprecise.

```{r}
#| label: fig-mechanism
#| fig-cap: "The partisan gap on the fact emerges first among the college-educated."
rd("fact_gap_by_education.csv") |>
  mutate(education = recode(education, college = "college", no_college = "no college")) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, gap, color = education, shape = education)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey70") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "year", y = "Rep - Dem gap", color = NULL, shape = NULL)
```

This sequence reconciles two facts that can look opposed: the partisan gap *emerges* first among graduates (here), yet it is non-college Democrats who ultimately *move* most (§6). They are two stages of one process (@fig-movement). College Democrats abandon the folk belief a decade before anyone else — opening the early gap among the educated — while non-college Democrats, starting from a far higher baseline (55 percent in 1996), peel away later but travel farther, to 18 percent by 2024 (a 37-point fall against the college Democrats' 24). Republicans of both education levels barely move throughout. The educated lead; the less-educated catch up and, from their higher start, cover the greater distance. First-mover and largest-mover are different roles, and Democrats of different educations play them in turn.

```{r}
#| label: fig-movement
#| fig-cap: "Who moved, and when: share agreeing 'immigrants take jobs', by party and education (GSS). College Democrats peel away first; non-college Democrats start higher, move later, and travel farther; both Republican groups barely move."
rd("fact_gap_by_education.csv") |>
  pivot_longer(c(dem_share, rep_share), names_to = "party", values_to = "share") |>
  mutate(party = recode(party, dem_share = "Democrats", rep_share = "Republicans"),
         education = recode(education, college = "college", no_college = "no college")) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, share, color = party, linetype = education)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.6)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Democrats = "#378ADD", Republicans = "#D85A30")) +
  labs(x = "year", y = "share agreeing \"immigrants take jobs\"", color = NULL, linetype = NULL)
```

## Confirmation in a second survey (ANES 2024)

The clean test comes from a different survey, a *behavioral* measure of sophistication, and many sampling units. In the 2024 ANES, the partisan gap on whether immigration is likely to take jobs *widens monotonically with political knowledge* — from thirty-four points among the least knowledgeable to forty-six among the most — and the design-based party-by-knowledge interaction is +0.51 (*p* \< .001; @tbl-anes, @fig-anes). The most informed Democrats are the *most* likely to reject the folk belief; informed Republicans do not move. An information-deficit account predicts the gap should shrink with knowledge; it does the reverse. The result is positive and significant across all twenty-four reasonable specifications (@fig-multiverse) [@simonsohn2020specification; @steegen2016multiverse], concentrates among strong partisans, and survives dropping the weights (Appendix B).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-anes
#| tbl-cap: "Partisan gap on 'immigrants take jobs' by political-knowledge level (ANES 2024)."
rd("anes_gap_by_knowledge.csv") |> kable(digits = 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-anes
#| fig-cap: "The gap widens with political knowledge — the opposite of an information-deficit prediction, and consistent with asymmetric motivated reasoning (party×knowledge +0.51, p < .001)."
rd("anes_gap_by_knowledge.csv") |>
  mutate(knowledge = factor(knowledge, levels = c("low (0-1)", "mid (2)", "high (3-4)"))) |>
  pivot_longer(c(dem_share, rep_share), names_to = "party", values_to = "share") |>
  mutate(party = recode(party, dem_share = "Democrats", rep_share = "Republicans")) |>
  ggplot(aes(knowledge, share, color = party, group = party)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.6)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Democrats = "#378ADD", Republicans = "#D85A30")) +
  labs(x = "political knowledge (0-4 correct)", y = "share agreeing", color = NULL)
```

## The amplification is borne by the out-group

The amplification is not symmetric across parties, and the asymmetry is itself informative. Decomposing the knowledge effect within each party (@tbl-knowledge-party), the slope of the folk belief on political knowledge is sharply negative among Democrats (log-odds −0.49, *p* \< .001) — the most knowledgeable Democrats hold the belief at seven percent against seventeen among the least — while among Republicans it is flat and insignificant (+0.04, *p* = .36). The two slopes differ decisively: a direct test of the difference (the party×knowledge interaction) returns +0.53, *p* \< .001, so the asymmetry is a tested quantity, not an eyeballed contrast. This bears on two rivals at once. Classic identity-protective cognition is *symmetric* — it predicts sophistication sharpens both poles [@kahan2012polarizing; @kahan2013ideology] — and a naïve account in which knowledge tracks the truth predicts both sides move toward the experts; the one-sidedness contradicts each. It is, instead, what the present model predicts: sophistication amplifies enactment of the identity prior $p(s)$, and for Republicans the party line coincides with the folk default, so capacity has nothing to add, while for Democrats the line departs from it, so knowledge carries them toward the experts.

We are careful about what the one-sidedness does *not* establish. It rules out symmetric cheerleading and naïve truth-tracking, but it does not adjudicate between motivated reasoning and *divergent information environments*, and we do not claim it does. Under the divergent-diets account the expert signal sits in the Democratic media diet and the folk-congruent signal in the Republican one, so the attentive of each side absorb opposite signals — reproducing the very one-sidedness we observe through exposure rather than cognition [@jerit2012partisan]. The asymmetry is therefore *consistent with* asymmetric motivated reasoning [@taber2006motivated] but does not identify it against selective exposure. Two observational controls narrow, without closing, the exposure channel: the party×knowledge interaction on the fact survives controlling for party×political-attention (+0.51 → +0.40) and, more to the point, for party×trust-in-media — a content-relevant proxy for which sources a partisan credits — falling only from +0.53 to +0.49 (*p* \< .001; @tbl-mediadiet). Differential trust in, and attention to, mainstream sources does not account for the amplification; but neither control measures the *content* of consumption directly, and only the pre-registered incentivized-accuracy experiment (Appendix E) can separate cognition from exposure cleanly. We therefore read "knowledge enacts the party line" as a description of the pattern — the better-informed move toward their party's pole, which for the out-group coincides with the experts — not as an identified claim that cognition rather than exposure produces it.

The aggregate counterpart is the one-sided movement of the capstone, though we are precise about its dynamics. Across the whole period the gap's growth is overwhelmingly Democratic (ninety-eight percent of the *net* 1996→2024 change), and the Democratic series falls monotonically; but the Republican series is not flat throughout — it drifts down through 2022 and then rises eleven points in 2024, so the most recent interval is roughly seventy percent Republican movement (§6, @tbl-gap-decomp). The in-group is thus better described as having moved little *on net* across three decades than as anchored in place. General *education*, by contrast, erodes the folk error on both sides (on trade as on immigration the college-educated hold it less, consistent with P2) — which is the point: it is *political knowledge*, the capacity to recognize and apply the party line, that moves the out-group alone. The same asymmetry, at far larger scale, governs the matched immigration preference in the Cooperative Election Study (≈ 38,000 respondents per survey; party×education interaction +0.38 to +0.80; Appendix B), so the machinery is not a small-sample artifact.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-knowledge-party
#| tbl-cap: "Within-party decomposition: political knowledge moves Democrats toward the experts but leaves Republicans flat (ANES 2024; survey-weighted logit of the folk belief on standardized knowledge, within party)."
rd("anes_knowledge_by_party.csv") |>
  kable(digits = 3, col.names = c("Party", "Belief, low knowledge", "Belief, high knowledge",
                                  "Knowledge (log-odds)", "p", "n"))
```

## Why knowledge, not just education

Does the result depend on the ANES or on its particular sophistication measure? It recurs in the GSS, with education in place of the knowledge battery — but through a revealingly different door (@tbl-education-by-party). Across the high-tribalization years (2014–2024), education lowers the folk belief in *both* parties: Democrats from 24 to 10 percent across the college line, Republicans from 42 to 32. General schooling is the classic corrector of folk-economic error, and it corrects everyone. It corrects Democrats about twice as steeply (a within-party log-odds of −1.04 against −0.44), so the partisan gap still widens with education — from 19 points among non-graduates to 22 among graduates — though only modestly. Political knowledge in the ANES does something sharper: it leaves Republicans flat and moves only Democrats, widening the gap from 34 to 46 points.

The contrast is not a discrepancy but a prediction of the model, and it is why the decisive test is the knowledge interaction rather than the education one. Education acts on the folk prior $f(s)$, common to both parties, and pulls both toward the experts; political knowledge — the capacity to recognize and enact the party line — acts on $p(s)$, which departs from folk intuition only for the out-group. A measure of general human capital therefore corrects the shared error in everyone and sorts only weakly; a measure of party-line enactment isolates the identity channel and sorts sharply. Two surveys and two measures point the same way, and they differ exactly as the two-channel model says they should: in whether the in-group is corrected (by schooling) or left where its party sits (under political knowledge).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-education-by-party
#| tbl-cap: "GSS within-party education slopes on the immigration fact (2014–2024). Education corrects both parties — unlike ANES political knowledge, which moves only the out-group — but corrects Democrats about twice as steeply."
rd("gss_education_by_party.csv") |>
  kable(digits = 3, col.names = c("Party", "No college", "College", "Education (log-odds)", "n"))
```

## Robustness: multiverse and heterogeneity

```{r}
#| label: spec-curve
#| results: asis
.scp <- file.path(proc, "anes_spec_curve.csv")
if (file.exists(.scp)) {
  sc <- readr::read_csv(.scp, show_col_types = FALSE)
  cat(sprintf("Across %d specifications the party$\\times$knowledge interaction is positive in %.0f%% and significant (p<.05) in %.0f%% (coefficients %.2f--%.2f).",
              nrow(sc), mean(sc$coef > 0) * 100, mean(sc$coef > 0 & sc$p < .05) * 100,
              min(sc$coef), max(sc$coef)))
} else cat("*[Multiverse pending --- run `Rscript run_all.R` to generate `anes_spec_curve.csv`.]*")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-multiverse
#| fig-cap: "Specification curve: the party×knowledge interaction across 24 specifications (sorted; purple = p < .05)."
rd("anes_spec_curve.csv") |>
  arrange(coef) |> mutate(rank = row_number(), sig = p < .05) |>
  ggplot(aes(rank, coef, color = sig)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, color = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#534AB7", `FALSE` = "grey70"),
                     labels = c(`TRUE` = "p < .05", `FALSE` = "n.s.")) +
  labs(x = "specification (sorted by coefficient)",
       y = "party x knowledge interaction (log-odds)", color = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-strength
#| tbl-cap: "Heterogeneity: Rep–Dem gap on the fact by knowledge level, within partisan strength (ANES 2024)."
rd("anes_het_strength.csv") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = klev, values_from = gap) |>
  select(strength, low, high) |>
  kable(digits = 2, col.names = c("Partisan strength", "Low-knowledge gap", "High-knowledge gap"))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-het-age
#| tbl-cap: "Heterogeneity: party×knowledge interaction by age cohort (ANES 2024)."
rd("anes_het_age.csv") |> kable(digits = 3, col.names = c("Age cohort", "Interaction (log-odds)", "n"))
```

## Out-of-sample replication

The multiverse establishes that the 2024 interaction is robust *within* its survey; it cannot establish that the result is not peculiar to that survey or to the four-item battery. The ANES Time Series Cumulative File lets us check both at once. It carries the identical "take jobs" fact, harmonized across years (`VCF9223`), together with a *different* sophistication measure — the interviewer's rating of the respondent's general level of political information — fielded in the earlier, fully in-person waves. Re-estimating the party×sophistication interaction on the fact thus replicates the result out of sample in two senses simultaneously: a different operationalization of sophistication, in different survey-years. It reproduces cleanly (@tbl-cdf-replication): the interaction is +0.39 in 2008, +0.40 in 2012, and +0.52 in 2016 — the last essentially the 2024 magnitude — and +0.41 pooled (p ≈ 10⁻¹⁰). It is, tellingly, *absent* in 2004 (+0.05, n.s.): before immigration had hardened along party lines, sophistication did not amplify the gap, exactly the conditional law the theory predicts (P2/P3) — amplification appears only once the issue tribalizes. The headline mechanism is therefore neither a one-survey nor a one-instrument artifact; it recurs across four surveys and two distinct sophistication measures, and switches off in the pre-tribalization year as the model requires.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cdf-replication
#| tbl-cap: "Out-of-sample replication (ANES Cumulative File): party×political-information interaction on the immigration 'take jobs' fact, using the interviewer's information rating in place of the behavioral battery. Present once the issue tribalizes (2008–2016), absent before (2004)."
rd("anes_cdf_replication.csv") |>
  kable(digits = 3, col.names = c("Year", "Interaction (log-odds)", "p", "n"))
```

## Scope: sophistication amplifies only in the identity regime

The mechanism is bounded, not universal — sophistication does not make people polarize on everything. Using education as a common sophistication measure across surveys, the party×education interaction on the folk belief is null where the issue is untribalized (automation), *negative* where education still corrects the folk error (AI), and positive where the issue is tribalized (immigration; @tbl-falsification). Sophistication thus plays opposite roles in the two regimes: it *corrects* the folk error where party is not engaged and *defends* the party line where it is. We are direct about the limits of this particular table: the predicted positive cell — the immigration party×education interaction — is positive (+0.337) but does *not* clear significance (*p* = .27), while the AI cell is significantly negative; so the gradient runs in the predicted *direction* across the three issues but is not a monotonic-with-significance pattern. We therefore present @tbl-falsification as supporting scope evidence rather than a clean law — the education-based estimates are individually noisy, and within immigration the amplification weakens after 2014 as the sorting diffuses beyond graduates (@fig-mechanism) — and we let the design-clean ANES knowledge result (the directly tested asymmetry, robust to education, ideology, racial-resentment, and media-trust controls; @tbl-knowledge-controls, @tbl-resentment-controls, @tbl-mediadiet) carry the primary weight.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-falsification
#| tbl-cap: "Scope of the mechanism: party×education amplification of the folk belief by tribalization. Null at low tribalization, correcting at low-mid, amplifying at high."
rd("falsification.csv") |>
  kable(digits = 3, col.names = c("Claim", "Tribalization", "party×education", "p", "n"))
```

## The structural signature: the sophistication premium is itself a product of tribalization

The model's gap equation, $\text{Gap}(s) = (1-\alpha)\,g(T)\,(p_R(s)-p_D(s))$, is *multiplicatively separable*, and that separability makes a prediction sharper than anything tested so far. Two of its quantities are observable over time on the same fact: the mass partisan gap — the $g(T)$ term — and the *sophistication premium*, the party×sophistication interaction, which is $\partial\,\text{Gap}/\partial s$ and which the model makes proportional to $g(T)$ as well. Ordinary issue-evolution predicts the gap should grow as elites polarize an issue. The two-regime model predicts something issue-evolution does not: the sophistication premium should grow *with it*, from zero before tribalization — the cross-derivative $\partial^2\text{Gap}/\partial s\,\partial T > 0$. The premium is not a standing trait of the sophisticated; it should switch on as the issue tribalizes.

It does. Taking the immigration "take jobs" fact across the years the elite-tribalization series covers (ANES Cumulative, 2004–2016) and measuring sophistication by the interviewer's political-information rating, both quantities move together with elite tribalization (@fig-structural). In 2004, before immigration tribalized, both are essentially zero — the mass gap is $-0.04$ and the sophistication premium is $+0.05$ (n.s.). As elite tribalization rises across 2008–2016, both rise in step: the mass gap to $+0.23$ and the premium to $+0.52$, tracking the elite series at correlations of $+0.86$ and $+0.91$, and each other at $+0.85$. The sophistication premium is, empirically, a product of the issue's tribalization, exactly as the multiplicative $g(T)$ structure requires — and this is the feature that separates the model from a generic account in which the gap merely widens.

One further detail confirms the *channel* structure rather than muddying it. The same premium measured by general *education* instead of political information does not switch on with tribalization — it is already large in 1996, before the cleavage. That is the right behavior under the model, not a contradiction: education acts on the folk prior $f(s)$, which is present and corrigible in *both* regimes, whereas political information acts on the identity term $p(s)$, which enters only through $g(T)$. The two sophistication measures diverge precisely because the model says they tap different channels. We hold this result to the same modest standard as the precedence analysis it complements: four survey-years are a descriptive pattern, anchored by the clean 2004 null, not a powered estimate — but the pattern is the functional form of the theory, visible in the data.

```{r}
#| label: fig-structural
#| fig-cap: "The multiplicative structure, made visible. On the immigration fact (ANES Cumulative 2004–2016), the mass partisan gap and the sophistication premium (party×political-information interaction) both rise from ~zero in step with elite tribalization — the $g(T)$ term and its sophistication-derivative scaling together, as $\\text{Gap}=(1-\\alpha)\\,g(T)\\,\\Delta p(s)$ predicts."
rd("structural_signature.csv") |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(mass_gap, sophistication_premium), names_to = "quantity", values_to = "value") |>
  dplyr::mutate(quantity = dplyr::recode(quantity,
        mass_gap = "mass partisan gap",
        sophistication_premium = "sophistication premium")) |>
  ggplot(aes(elite_tribalization, value, color = quantity, shape = quantity)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey75") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) + geom_point(size = 2.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = year), color = "grey40", size = 3, vjust = -0.9, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("mass partisan gap" = "#D85A30",
                                "sophistication premium" = "#534AB7")) +
  labs(x = "elite tribalization T (congressional immigration speech)",
       y = "value", color = NULL, shape = NULL)
```

## Beyond immigration, and beyond economics

If the account is right, immigration is not special. The mechanism is defined by the *structure* of a claim — truth-apt, unverifiable from ordinary experience, contested by elites, with a folk default that one party's pole shares — not by its content, so it should appear on any belief with that structure, in any domain. It does. Consider a fact from outside economics entirely: whether human beings evolved from earlier species of animals. The scientific consensus is all but universal; the claim is unverifiable from everyday life; the folk default — that humans are not animals — is just the kind of pre-political intuition the model places at $f$; and elites have contested it along partisan and religious lines. The GSS science module fields it (`evolved`) from 2006 to 2018, and every signature of the immigration result reappears (@fig-evolution). The Republican–Democrat gap in *disbelief* grows from fourteen points in 2006 to twenty-four in 2018, and it grows one-sidedly, exactly as on immigration: Democrats converge on the scientific consensus (disbelief falls from 43 to 34 percent) while Republicans anchor at the folk default (essentially flat, 57 to 58 percent). A sophistication signature appears here too — the party-by-education interaction on disbelief is +0.59 (*p* = .001) — but it does not survive the obvious confound, and we report that plainly rather than let a referee find it. Disbelief in evolution is heavily structured by religiosity, which is itself correlated with party; once we control for church attendance and biblical literalism and their interactions with party, the party-by-education interaction falls to +0.21 and loses significance (*p* = .15). So we make a deliberately narrower claim for this case than for immigration. Evolution corroborates the *capture* — a non-economic fact acquiring a partisan structure, asymmetrically, over two decades — which is the generalization that matters: the phenomenon is not confined to economics or to immigration. But its sophistication-amplification is entangled with religiosity in a way the immigration result (where the knowledge interaction survives attention controls, §7) is not, so we lean on evolution for the partisanization itself, not as independent evidence for the sophistication mechanism. The series is also short (seven waves, ending 2018) and measured by education rather than the behavioral knowledge battery. The Time-Traveller's Problem is not a fact about one issue; it is a fact about belief under unverifiability, and economics is its cleanest laboratory, not its only one.

```{r}
#| label: fig-evolution
#| fig-cap: "The same capture, a different domain: the partisan gap on whether humans evolved (GSS science module, 2006–2018). Disbelief sorts by party — Democrats converging on the scientific consensus, Republicans anchored at the folk default — exactly as on immigration."
rd("evolution_partisan_gap.csv") |>
  pivot_longer(c(dem_share, rep_share), names_to = "party", values_to = "share") |>
  mutate(party = recode(party, dem_share = "Democrats", rep_share = "Republicans")) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, share, color = party)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.7)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Democrats = "#378ADD", Republicans = "#D85A30")) +
  labs(x = "year", y = "share disbelieving humans evolved", color = NULL)
```

## Content neutrality: when Republicans are the out-group

Both cases worked so far — immigration and evolution — have the *same* party, the Democrats, moving toward the credentialed-expert position. That pattern is observationally consistent with a simpler and less interesting claim than ours: that Democrats are merely more deferential to expert and scientific consensus. Our model asserts something content-free and stronger — that the converging out-group is *whichever* party's pole departs from the folk default, regardless of which party that is. The decisive evidence is a case in which the folk default is the Democratic-congenial position and the experts side with the Republicans; trade supplies one. Folk economics marks the protectionist, anti-foreign-trade intuition as the shared default [@caplan2007myth]; the experts hold the opposite, that trade raises aggregate welfare. On the ANES import-limits item, the party sitting at the protectionist folk default is *not* fixed — it switches (@fig-trade-flip). From 1988 through 2012, Democrats were the more protectionist party (the Republican–Democrat gap in favoring import limits ran from −3 to −11 points): the anti-market folk position was the Democratic one, and the expert-aligned, freer-trade side was Republican. By 2016 the gap had flipped to +13 points and by 2024 to +42, as the Trump-era Republican Party adopted the protectionist line and Democrats moved toward the economists. The party that holds the folk-economic error against the experts is therefore set by the structure of elite conflict, not by a standing disposition of one party to defer: before 2016, on a market belief, it is the *Republicans* who occupy the expert-aligned pole that the model assigns to the out-group. This is the content neutrality the immigration and evolution cases alone could not establish. We are precise about its limit: because trade tribalized only *after* the parties exchanged positions, its low-tribalization era (when Republicans were the expert-aligned side) is one in which sophistication corrects the folk error in *both* parties (the P2 regime, as in §6), so trade demonstrates content neutrality through the *direction and flip of the partisan gap* rather than through a sophistication-amplification test with Republicans as the converging side — the latter would require a market fact that is both expert-Republican-congenial and strongly tribalized, which we flag in the limitations as the remaining step.

```{r}
#| label: fig-trade-flip
#| fig-cap: "Content neutrality. On the ANES import-limits item, the protectionist (folk-economic) default is held by Democrats from 1988–2012 and by Republicans after 2016: the party that departs from the experts is set by elite conflict, not by a fixed disposition to defer. Share favoring limits on imports, by party."
rd("trade_content_neutrality.csv") |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(dem_protectionist, rep_protectionist), names_to = "party", values_to = "share") |>
  dplyr::mutate(party = dplyr::recode(party, dem_protectionist = "Democrats", rep_protectionist = "Republicans")) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, share, color = party)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Democrats = "#378ADD", Republicans = "#D85A30")) +
  labs(x = "year", y = "share favoring limits on imports (folk/protectionist)", color = NULL)
```

## Cross-national scope: capture follows elite supply, not the number of parties

The mechanism is built on the two-party United States, which raises a scope question: should fact-capture be weaker where many parties and coalition government diffuse the partisan signal? We test the conjecture with the ISSP 2013 National Identity module [@issp2013ni], which fields the *same* economic fact — whether "immigrants take jobs away from people born in [country]" — in twenty-six democracies, alongside a harmonized left–right party-family measure. For each country we take the left–right gap in the folk belief (the right bloc's rate of agreement minus the left's; @fig-issp). Three results follow, and the third is not the one we expected.

First, the capture generalizes: the gap is positive — the right holds the folk belief more — in seventy-seven percent of the twenty-six countries. A truth-apt immigration fact carries an ideological signature across most democracies, not only in the polarized United States. Second, the naive scope conjecture *fails*: the gap is uncorrelated with party-system fragmentation (the effective number of parliamentary parties; *r* = +0.16, *p* = .44, the wrong sign for "weaker under multi-party systems"). Belgium, with eight effective parties, shows a larger gap than the two-party United States; Sweden, also highly fragmented, shows almost none. Multi-party systems do not capture the fact less.

Third, what *does* track the gap is elite issue-supply. The left–right gap is roughly four times larger in countries with a salient anti-immigration party (mean 0.13) than in those without one (0.03; a difference that is statistically reliable, Welch *t* = 2.96, *p* = .01, and survives controlling for the number of parties, *p* = .006) — capture appears wherever an elite party *owns* the folk position, regardless of how many parties compete. We flag one important caveat: this moderator is plausibly *endogenous* to the very capture we measure, since a party's ownership of the anti-immigration position and the partisan sorting of the immigration fact are co-determined and may be two faces of one process rather than cause and effect. We therefore read the contrast as descriptive corroboration, not as an identified moderator. With that caveat, it refines the scope condition rather than confirming it, and in doing so it corroborates the paper's deeper claim: capture is driven from the elite level (the precedence result of §6), so it requires a party to carry the folk pole, not a particular number of parties. The United States is instructive precisely because it is *mid-ranked* (ninth of twenty-six) in 2013 — exactly what its own GSS series implies, since the US immigration gap was only about eight points in 2014 and reached thirty-three only by 2024. A single cross-national snapshot therefore compares countries at different points in their own tribalization, which is itself a caution we carry into the reading. The honest conclusion is that the identity mechanism is not confined to two-party systems, that it does not weaken with party number as we had conjectured, and that its cross-national footprint is set by whether elites supply a party to own the unverifiable claim.

```{r}
#| label: fig-issp
#| fig-cap: "Cross-national scope (ISSP 2013, 26 democracies). Left–right gap on the 'immigrants take jobs' fact against party-system fragmentation (effective number of parliamentary parties). The gap is positive in most countries but is *uncorrelated* with the number of parties (r = +0.16, n.s.); it is larger where a salient anti-immigration party exists (orange). The US (two-party) is mid-ranked, consistent with its still-rising GSS trajectory in 2013."
rd("issp_crossnational.csv") |>
  mutate(`anti-immigration party` = ifelse(salient_antiimmig_party == 1, "salient", "none")) |>
  ggplot(aes(enp, gap_right_minus_left, color = `anti-immigration party`)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey70") +
  geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = country), size = 3, vjust = -0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(salient = "#D85A30", none = "#534AB7")) +
  labs(x = "effective number of parliamentary parties (~2013)",
       y = "right − left gap on 'immigrants take jobs'")
```

# Discussion

The organizing claim is that economic belief under unverifiability runs in two regimes, and that an issue can move from one to the other within a generation. Where a claim is uncontested, citizens hold a shared folk-economic error that information and mechanism-explanation can move toward the experts [@meyers2020inducing; @meyers2023broad]. Where a claim is contested, information no longer converges belief: it carries the out-group toward the experts while leaving the in-group in place, so that more of it *widens* the partisan gap rather than closing it — because the obstacle is not a deficit of knowledge but a surplus of identity [@kahan2012polarizing; @sapienza2013economic]. The VOTER panel shows this transition is not merely a property of shifting aggregates but of individuals: the same people, no better able to check the claim than before, revised it into partisan line as the issue tribalized, and their prior partisanship forecast the revision more than their prior belief forecast their partisanship.

We are deliberate about the epistemic status of the two-regime model relative to the findings. The descriptive results are the secure core, and they are novel on their own terms: a truth-apt, fixed-wording economic fact migrated into the partisan structure a matched preference already held (from nine to seventy-two percent of it), reaching value-cleavage magnitude; the same structure recurs on evolution, on trade through a directional party-flip, and across twenty-six democracies; and the partisan gap and the sophistication premium co-scale with elite tribalization. The formal model earns its keep by *organizing* these regularities into one gap equation and by sharpening the mechanism test — but its single genuinely derived prediction, the content-free claim that the converging out-group is whichever party departs from the folk default, is only partially borne out: the trade flip confirms it on the direction of the gap, but the sophistication-amplified version with Republicans as the converging side remains untested, and the folk-default anchoring is pinned partly by which party stayed put. We therefore present the model as an organizing lens rather than a validated structural object, read the mechanism as consistent with — not as identifying — asymmetric motivated reasoning against selective exposure, and assign the work of identification to the pre-registered experiment. The paper's claims, in short, are exactly as strong as the design: a demonstrated and general descriptive phenomenon, organized by a model whose deepest prediction awaits one more test.

This is the answer to the question in the title. How do you convince someone of a claim they cannot check? It depends which regime they are in. On an uncontested claim, supply the mechanism: explanation moves belief toward the experts. On a contested one, information is the wrong tool; the only levers the theory implies are de-tribalization or a trusted in-group messenger who can carry an unverifiable fact across the partisan filter. We offer this last as a conjecture the theory licenses, not a finding the data establish — its test is the pre-registered experiment of Appendix E — and we note that partisan media plausibly act not as a competing cause but as the high-gain amplifier of the elite signal, consistent with the precedence result.

The reach of the argument extends well beyond economics, and §7 has already shown it: the partisan capture of disbelief in evolution — a fact with no economic content whatever — reproduces every feature of the immigration result, down to the asymmetry and the sophistication amplification. The Time-Traveller's Problem is a general condition, not a feature of immigration or of dollars: it arises wherever a truth-apt claim is unverifiable from ordinary experience and contested by elites — the trajectory of the climate, the effects of public-health measures, the consequences of a distant war, the safety of a new technology. In each such domain the model predicts that belief will be governed by identity rather than evidence, that the governance will be asymmetric and sophistication-amplified, and that which facts are captured will track the unverifiable and the tribalizing; the evolution case is one such domain already in hand, and it behaves exactly as predicted. Economics is merely the cleanest laboratory — it supplies a credentialed expert benchmark and long runs of fixed-wording items — but the phenomenon it exposes is a property of belief under unverifiability as such. Naming it is part of the contribution: fact capture, under the Time-Traveller's Problem, is a recurring mode by which mass publics come to hold party-sorted beliefs about things they cannot check, and it should be found, and can be predicted, wherever those conditions recur.

The finding also refines the rationality debate. The public is not uniformly irrational in the manner of rational irrationality [@caplan2007myth]; it is *conditionally* so — rational-as-identity-management precisely where evidence cannot bind, and most so among those best able to reason. And it issues a caution to the civic-knowledge tradition: on contested facts, political knowledge does not bring the parties together but drives them apart, correcting the out-group while leaving the in-group unmoved. The remedy for misinformation cannot simply be more information: on a captured fact, more information sharpens the partisan divide even as it pulls one side toward the experts.

# Limitations and scope

We state the design's boundaries plainly, as scope conditions on what the evidence licenses rather than as grounds to discount it. The precedence of elite over mass polarization is an instance of issue evolution, framed as confirmation not discovery — and it is estimated on the immigration *preference*, which has the biennial waves a lead–lag requires, not on the five-wave fact; that facts undergo *elite-led* issue evolution is therefore an inference from the preference's precedence, the cross-sectional gradient, and the fact's emergence first among the sophisticated (§7), not a lead–lag estimated on the fact itself. The mechanism is read as *consistent with* asymmetric motivated reasoning: the sophistication interaction adjudicates against an information-deficit account, and three further steps narrow the divergent-diets and confound alternatives (the party-by-knowledge interaction on the fact survives controlling for political attention; it survives party-by-racial-resentment and party-by-authoritarianism — the immigration analog of the religiosity control that dissolved the evolution sophistication effect, §7; and political knowledge moves only the out-group toward the experts, not the in-group, as truth-tracking would), but no observational design *completely* separates identity-protective cognition from party-correlated exposure (§5), a separation the pre-registered experiment is built to finish. The behavioral-knowledge interaction on the fact was first estimated on a single 2024 cross-section, but it now replicates out of sample: the specification curve establishes its robustness within 2024 to party coding, controls, weighting, and the belief cutpoint; the GSS education trajectory and the CES corroborate the mechanism cross-survey; and in the ANES cumulative file the same party×sophistication amplification of the take-jobs fact appears in 2008, 2012, and 2016 using the interviewer's information rating in place of the behavioral battery — and is absent in pre-tribalization 2004, as the conditional law requires (§7). What remains genuinely owed is the narrower step of reproducing the interaction with the same behavioral-knowledge battery and fact item in a second survey. Verifiability is a theoretical lens, not an identified moderator, and we are blunt that it does no within-sample identifying work: every studied claim is low-verifiability, so the design identifies the *tribalization* comparative statics (P2–P5) while verifiability enters only as a scope condition certified by the index. Indeed, within our three claims verifiability does not even order the capture — immigration is the most checkable (CVI 6 of 12) yet the most captured — which is consistent with the model (capture runs through the $g(T)$ tribalization channel, not the $\alpha(v)$ channel, once all claims are unverifiable enough) but means the $\alpha(v)$ term and the Time-Traveller framing it motivates are, empirically, an organizing scope condition rather than a tested moderator. The verifiability half-life is accordingly held apart from the numbered predictions — stated but untested here, for want of within-claim variation in checkability — with the prospective AI study (Appendix E), where employment effects grow observable as the technology deploys, designed to supply exactly that variation (H4). The design is observational. We make no causal claim about the direction between the fact and the matched *preference*; on the prior question of whether party leads the fact or the fact leads party, the VOTER panel's cross-lagged estimates point to party leading the within-person change in the belief (@sec-panel), though cross-lagged models recover lead–lag structure rather than strict causation, and the panel's belief item is a broader societal-contribution judgment than the verbatim economic fact. The over-time partisanization is shown directly on two facts from different domains — whether immigrants take jobs and, outside economics, whether humans evolved (§7) — so it is not a fact about one issue. We are nonetheless plain about how far this generality currently reaches. Within economics, the longitudinal evidence rests on two framings of a single underlying belief about immigration and the economy (`immjobs` and `immameco`, correlated at .95), not on two independent economic facts; the trade analog is not estimable (the GSS fielded its trade-and-jobs item only once), so the economic generality rests further on the cross-sectional gradient across three issues, on convergent evidence that partisan economic perceptions swing with the president's party [@bartels2002beyond], and on a registered forward prediction. The one *fully* independent domain, evolution, is a shorter series (seven waves to 2018) measured by education rather than the behavioral knowledge battery. The phenomenon is thus general in principle, and shown in two domains within the US; its cross-national breadth we now document directly with the ISSP (§7) — the immigration fact carries a left–right signature in most democracies — leaving the AI series, as it matures, as the remaining over-time extension. A distinct limit concerns *content*, not breadth, and it is the most consequential open test. In both fully-worked cases — immigration and evolution — the party that moves toward the credentialed-expert position is the Democratic one, so the evidence as it stands is observationally consistent with a simpler and less novel story in which Democrats are merely more deferential to expert and scientific consensus. The structural model claims something stronger and content-free: the converging out-group is whichever party's pole departs from the folk default, whichever party that is. The decisive test is a *market* fact whose folk anti-market default is Democratic-congenial and whose expert verdict is Republican-congenial — the employment effect of the minimum wage, rent control, the gains from trade — on which the model predicts that *Republicans* become the converging out-group. We establish this content neutrality at the level of the partisan gap's *direction*: on the ANES import-limits trade item (§7), the protectionist folk default is held by Democrats from 1988 through 2012 and by Republicans only after 2016, so before the Trump-era realignment the expert-aligned, freer-trade party on a market belief is the Republicans — the opposite party from immigration and evolution, which a fixed "Democrats defer to experts" account cannot accommodate. What trade cannot supply is the *sophistication-amplified* form of the test with Republicans as the converging side, because trade tribalized only after the parties exchanged positions, leaving its Republican-expert-aligned era in the low-tribalization regime where information corrects both parties. A market fact that is simultaneously expert-Republican-congenial and strongly tribalized — rent control, or the minimum wage's employment effect, with repeated public microdata and a sophistication measure — therefore remains the cleanest single extension; we flag it as such, and note that if the sophistication amplification failed to appear there, that too would be informative and would narrow the claim. The expressive-responding objection is met observationally but not experimentally, though the panel's durable nine-year within-person reversals are difficult to read as *momentary* cheerleading — durability is not itself sincerity, but it narrows the objection to its durable-expression form, which only the incentivized experiment can finally settle. The verifiability index is double-coded (Krippendorff's $\alpha = 0.88$; Appendix A), and certifies the design's premise rather than serving as a regressor. Finally, on the scope of the two-party setting: we had conjectured that the identity term should be weaker under multi-party, coalition systems, and the ISSP 2013 cross-national data (§7) let us put the conjecture to the test. It is not supported — the left–right gap on the immigration fact is uncorrelated with the number of parties (*r* = +0.16, n.s.) — but the capture itself generalizes (a right-more-folk gap in seventy-seven percent of twenty-six democracies) and tracks whether an elite party owns the anti-immigration position rather than the size of the party system. We therefore revise the condition rather than merely state it: the mechanism is not confined to two-party systems and does not weaken with party number; what it requires is an elite party to carry the folk pole, which is consistent with the precedence result. The one-shot cross-section also compares countries at different stages of their own tribalization — the United States is only mid-ranked in 2013, matching its GSS trajectory — so the cross-national reading is a snapshot rather than a dynamic test, and an over-time cross-national panel is the natural next step. None of these is fatal; each is a boundary the design draws openly, and several are the openings that the conclusion and the pre-registered designs of Appendix E turn into an agenda for future work.

# Conclusion

A truth-apt belief about the economy, its wording held fixed, came to sort by party nearly as strongly as a taste — and did so fastest among the citizens best equipped to know better. Followed as individuals across a decade, the same citizens revised a broad immigration-impact belief into partisan line, their party leading the change rather than trailing it. When a claim cannot be checked, belief tracks the identity of its source rather than the content of the message: the Time-Traveller's Problem. The next fact to sort is, the theory predicts, already visible in the data on artificial intelligence. Whether the discipline can find ways to carry unverifiable facts across the partisan filter — through mechanism, through messenger, through de-tribalization — is the question this diagnosis leaves for the work to come.

# Appendix A — Claim Verifiability Index

Each studied claim is scored 0–3 on four dimensions and summed to a 0–12 index; the anchors for each level are:

| Dimension | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| Temporal lag | resolves in \< 1 yr | 1–3 yr | 3–10 yr | \> 10 yr |
| Counterfactual dependence | direct comparison available | weak counterfactual | strong counterfactual required | inherently unobservable counterfactual |
| Attributional diffuseness | single clear cause | few competing causes | many competing causes | causally over-determined |
| Personal unobservability | verifiable from own experience | partly observable | rarely observable | never personally observable |

The index certifies that the studied claims are genuinely difficult to verify — the premise of the design — and is not used as a regressor; the studied claims cluster at the high end (mean 9.5 on the 0–12 scale; @tbl-cvi). Following standard practice for content-analytic measures [@krippendorff2004content], all seventeen claims were scored independently by a second coder applying the same rubric. Agreement is high: across the sixty-eight dimension-level ratings the two coders agree exactly 88 percent of the time and never differ by more than one point, giving Krippendorff's $\alpha = 0.88$ on the ordinal dimensions (and $\alpha = 0.98$ on the summed index) — comfortably above the pre-registered $\alpha \geq 0.67$ threshold for adequate agreement (the two codings are in `data/cvi_two_coders.csv`; the instrument is `data/cvi_coding_sheet.md`). The CVI is not used as a moderator because the studied claims lack the within-claim variation in verifiability that identifying a verifiability effect would require (the verifiability half-life held apart from the numbered predictions in the theory section).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cvi
#| tbl-cap: "Claim Verifiability Index scores (two independent coders; Krippendorff's α = 0.88 ordinal, 0.98 on totals)."
rd("cvi_scores.csv") |> kable(digits = 0)
```

# Appendix B — Robustness

The headline mechanism result is robust to specification, weighting, and coding.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-spec-full
#| tbl-cap: "Full specification curve: the party×knowledge interaction (log-odds) and p-value across all 24 specifications."
rd("anes_spec_curve.csv") |>
  transmute(belief = dc, party = pc, controls = ctrl, weighting = wtopt,
            coef = round(coef, 3), p = signif(p, 2)) |>
  kable()
```

The procedure follows specification-curve and multiverse practice [@simonsohn2020specification; @steegen2016multiverse]: rather than defend a single model, we report the full distribution of estimates across defensible analytic choices. Three points follow. First, every specification yields a positive, significant interaction (@fig-multiverse and the table above), so the result is not an artifact of a particular control set or coding. Second, the estimate is essentially unchanged with the survey weights removed, so it is not an artifact of the weighting. Third, the fact–preference coupling holds for both the older levels item (`letin1`) and the newer reduce item (`letin1a`) (@fig-coupling), so the stable-coupling result is not an artifact of item wording. Throughout, each survey is analyzed with its own native design weights; no single weight is pooled across surveys.

Two further caveats. The precedence test rests on eleven biennial observations; its lead–lag correlation and Granger-style coefficient are reported as suggestive temporal ordering, not as a powered time-series result, and we do not subject so short a series to unit-root or cointegration testing, which it cannot support. In place of asymptotic inference we use a time-shift randomization that respects autocorrelation: we correlate the public gap against the elite series displaced by every lag in a wide window and rank the observed ten-year alignment within that distribution. The lag-ten correlation falls near the ninetieth percentile (*p* ≈ .10) — consistent with elites leading, but conservative enough that we claim only ordering, not a precise lag or an effect size. This randomization is the appropriate small-sample replacement for the asymptotic Granger *p*, and it is deliberately the weaker of the two figures we report. Second, the `immjobs` item was fielded in 1996, 2004, 2014, 2022, and 2024 — not in 2021 — so the GSS's partial shift to web administration in 2021 does not enter the capstone series. The one notable irregularity, the 2022 GSS education split, is visible in @fig-mechanism and does not affect the design-based interaction or the cross-survey ANES confirmation. Across the five capstone waves the `immjobs` item was administered to comparable, randomly assigned ballot subsamples, with analytic Republican and Democratic counts per wave reported in @tbl-fact-gap (ranging from roughly 480 to 960 per party); the trend is not an artifact of the irregular spacing of fielding years, and — as §6 notes — the split-ballot structure is precisely why we retire the earlier within-person "fusion" reading in favor of the partisan-loading result.

## Wording robustness: a second immigration-economy fact

A natural worry is that the partisanization is an artifact of the specific phrase "immigrants take jobs." It is not. The GSS fields a second, differently framed claim about the same underlying fact — whether immigrants are, on balance, good for the American economy (`immameco`) — in 1996, 2004, 2014, and 2024. Its partisan gap follows an all-but-identical path (@fig-wording): flat through 2004, opening by 2014, and reaching twenty-two points by 2024, driven by the same one-sided movement — the share of Democrats calling immigrants good for the economy rises from 68 to 94 percent while Republicans barely move. The two fact-item gap trajectories correlate at *r* = .95 across the four common years. The capture is a property of the belief about immigration and the economy, not of any one item's wording.

```{r}
#| label: fig-wording
#| fig-cap: "Wording robustness: the partisan gap on a differently worded immigration-economy fact (whether immigrants are *not* good for the economy, immameco) tracks the gap on 'immigrants take jobs' (r = .95 across the four common years; GSS)."
rd("fact_wording_robustness.csv") |>
  ggplot(aes(year, gap, color = item, shape = item)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey75") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("immigrants take jobs" = "#D85A30",
                                "immigrants not good for economy" = "#534AB7")) +
  labs(x = "year", y = "Rep − Dem partisan gap", color = NULL, shape = NULL)
```

## Mechanism specificity: knowledge, not its correlates

A natural objection to the mechanism is that "political knowledge" is merely a proxy for education or ideology, so the knowledge×party interaction would vanish once those interactions are included. It does not. The interaction retains essentially its full magnitude and high significance controlling for party×education and party×ideology, while both of those interactions are themselves null — it is specifically political sophistication, not its correlates, that amplifies the sorting.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-knowledge-controls
#| tbl-cap: "Party×knowledge interaction on the immigration fact, net of party×education and party×ideology (ANES 2024)."
rd("anes_knowledge_controls.csv") |> kable(digits = 3, col.names = c("Model", "party×knowledge", "p", "n"))
```

A sharper version of the objection names a specific rival engine. For evolution we reported, against our own interest, that the sophistication signature did not survive religiosity: the party×education interaction on disbelief fell to non-significance once church attendance and biblical literalism and their party interactions entered (§7), because disbelief in evolution is largely structured by religiosity. The immigration analog of that confound is racial resentment (or authoritarianism): each is correlated with both party and political sophistication and is the natural alternative driver of immigration sorting. We therefore subject the knowledge×party interaction on the fact to the same kind of test, controlling for party×racial-resentment and party×authoritarianism (the four-item ANES batteries; racial resentment runs, as expected, far higher among Republicans). Unlike the evolution case, it survives: the interaction falls only from a log-odds of 0.53 to 0.46 with party×racial-resentment, to 0.41 with party×authoritarianism, and to 0.38 with both, remaining significant at p < .01 throughout (@tbl-resentment-controls). The amplification of immigration-fact sorting by political knowledge is not racial resentment, or authoritarianism, wearing a sophistication mask — which is the most important thing the contrast with evolution establishes, and the reason we ran the test that evolution failed.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-resentment-controls
#| tbl-cap: "The party×knowledge interaction on the immigration fact survives party×racial-resentment and party×authoritarianism (ANES 2024; survey-weighted logit, cluster-robust by PSU) — unlike the evolution sophistication effect, which did not survive its religiosity analog."
rd("anes_resentment_controls.csv") |> kable(digits = 3, col.names = c("Model", "party×knowledge (log-odds)", "p", "n"))
```

The divergent-information-environments account is the harder rival, because it predicts the same one-sided amplification through *exposure* rather than cognition (§5, §7). We cannot identify against it observationally, but we can test whether the readiest content-relevant proxy absorbs the interaction. Mainstream-media trust is sharply party-stratified (Democrats credit traditional news far more than Republicans do) and is the natural channel through which divergent diets would operate. Controlling for party×trust-in-media leaves the party×knowledge interaction essentially intact — 0.53 to 0.49 — and adding party×political-attention does no more (@tbl-mediadiet). This narrows the exposure account: the amplification is not reducible to *which* sources a partisan trusts or *how much* politics they follow. It does not close it, since neither measure captures the content of consumption directly; that separation is left to the experiment.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mediadiet
#| tbl-cap: "The party×knowledge interaction on the immigration fact survives controlling for party×media-trust, a content-relevant exposure proxy (ANES 2024; survey-weighted logit, cluster-robust by PSU). It narrows but does not close the divergent-diets account."
rd("anes_mediadiet_controls.csv") |> kable(digits = 3, col.names = c("Model", "party×knowledge (log-odds)", "p", "n"))
```

## The mechanism at scale (CES)

The asymmetric amplification is not an artifact of the ANES or of modest samples. In the Cooperative Election Study it replicates on the matched immigration *preference* at roughly thirty-eight thousand respondents per survey, across two years and three differently worded restrictionist items (@tbl-ces). On the cleanest item — support for reducing legal immigration by half, where neither party sits near a floor or a ceiling — education pulls Democrats toward openness about twice as steeply as Republicans (Democrats from 34 to 18 percent restrictionist across the college line, Republicans from 68 to 58), so the partisan gap *widens* with schooling and the party-by-education interaction is +0.38 (*p* \< 10⁻¹⁵). The 2024 items repeat the pattern (interactions +0.52 and +0.80), the only caveat being that Republican support for a border wall is near its ceiling, which mechanically limits in-group movement there. Two points follow. First, the mechanism the paper identifies on the fact — capacity recruited to enact the party line, moving the out-group while the in-group holds — is real and large beyond any sampling doubt. Second, the captured fact, having converged on the preference's partisanship (§6), is now driven by the very same machinery that governs the preference: the assimilation is complete in mechanism as well as in level. We are explicit about the boundary of this check, lest it be read for more than it is: it uses *education* on a *preference*, not the behavioral knowledge battery on the fact, so it confirms a related quantity rather than the headline one. Its scale, however, lets us take one observational step on the cognition-versus-exposure question of §5, which smaller samples cannot. If the amplification were merely party-correlated *exposure* — the more attentive of each side absorbing more of their own diet — then controlling for political attention should absorb it. It does not. Adding a party-by-political-attention interaction *halves* the party-by-education interaction but leaves it firmly significant (from +0.36 to +0.18 in the same respondents, *p* \< .001): education amplifies the partisan gap beyond what differential attention explains. This is not the incentivized experiment, and it does not isolate cognition completely, but it is more than a concession that exposure and capacity are indistinguishable — here, at n ≈ 38,000, they partly separate, and the part that survives belongs to capacity, not exposure. The same control run on the *headline* pairing — political knowledge and the fact, in the ANES — tells the same story (§7): the party-by-knowledge interaction falls only from +0.51 to +0.40 (*p* = .001) once party-by-attention is included. The CES contributes scale; the ANES contributes directness, applying the test to the very quantity the mechanism claim is about.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ces
#| tbl-cap: "The mechanism at scale (CES 2022–2024, n ≈ 38,000 each): the partisan gap on immigration restriction widens with education, driven by the out-group, across three items. Shares are the restrictionist share; the interaction is party×college (log-odds)."
rd("ces_mechanism.csv") |>
  transmute(Year = year, Item = item,
            `Dem (no coll → coll)` = paste0(dem_noncol, " → ", dem_col),
            `Rep (no coll → coll)` = paste0(rep_noncol, " → ", rep_col),
            `party×college` = interaction, p = p, n = n) |>
  kable()
```

## Behavior, against expressive responding

Expressive responding [@bullock2015partisan; @prior2015serious] holds that partisans may report beliefs they do not hold to cheer their side. The observational design cannot fully exclude this — the clean test is the deferred incentivized experiment (Appendix E) — but the factual belief carries independent political weight that pure cheerleading on a single survey item would not produce. In ANES 2024 it predicts consequential behavior, 2024 presidential vote and border-wall support, *net of party identification and political knowledge*:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-behavior
#| tbl-cap: "The factual belief predicts behavior net of party and knowledge (ANES 2024; odds ratios from survey-weighted logits)."
rd("anes_behavior.csv") |> kable(col.names = c("Outcome", "Fact OR", "p", "n"))
```

The sharpest form of the objection is that "net of party" under-models identity when party is only a three-category measure. The result does not depend on that coarseness. Re-estimating the fact's effect on presidential vote on a common sample while progressively adding seven-point party identification, then seven-point ideology, then knowledge, the odds ratio falls from roughly nine but stabilizes just above six and stays overwhelmingly significant (@tbl-behavior-controls): the belief predicts the vote at an odds ratio of about 6.1 net of a full identity battery. A report that tracked nothing but partisan identity should be largely absorbed by these controls; it is not.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-behavior-controls
#| tbl-cap: "The factual belief predicts presidential vote net of progressively richer identity controls (ANES 2024; odds ratio on the fact, survey-weighted logit)."
rd("anes_behavior_controls.csv") |>
  kable(col.names = c("Identity controls", "Fact OR", "p", "n"))
```

A belief that predicts the vote net of a rich identity battery shows that it travels with consequential partisan commitments — but, since a vote report is itself a self-report open to the same expressive pressures as the belief report, this does not by itself establish sincerity. Only the incentivized-accuracy experiment (Appendix E) can partition the sincere from the expressive component.

## The within-person panel (VOTER): cross-lagged direction and change-score

The within-person capture result (@sec-panel) rests on the Views of the Electorate Research (VOTER) panel, which re-interviewed the same national sample across 2011–2020; the belief item asks whether immigrants "mostly make a contribution to American society" or are "mostly a drain," coded so that higher values are the anti-immigrant (folk) direction, and party is the seven-point identification at each wave. Both variables are standardized within the analysis sample.

The headline estimate is the random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) of @hamaker2015critique, fit by maximum likelihood on the complete four-wave sample (2011, 2016, 2018, 2020; n = 2{,}008 full-participation respondents; RMSEA = 0.067). A pair of random intercepts absorbs each respondent's stable trait level in party and in belief, so the cross-lagged paths describe *within-person* deviations rather than between-person differences — the correction the two-wave CLPM cannot make. Cross-lags are constrained equal across waves (a conservative simplification given the unequal 5/2/2-year spacing). The within-person party→belief path (0.40) exceeds the belief→party path (0.12), and a nonparametric bootstrap of the difference (300 resamples) places it at 0.28 with a 95% interval of [0.19, 0.38] that excludes zero in every resample (@tbl-voter-riclpm). Two simpler estimators agree: the ordinary two-wave standardized CLPM (2011→2020) gives party→belief 0.33 versus belief→party 0.20, and a change-score regression of the 2011→2020 belief change on 2011 party — which differences out each respondent's baseline — gives β = 0.12 (p < .001). That the asymmetry is *larger*, not smaller, once trait variance is partialled out is the reverse of what an artifact-of-stable-dispositions reading predicts.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-voter-riclpm
#| tbl-cap: "Random-intercept cross-lagged panel model on the VOTER panel (four waves 2011–2020, standardized; RI-CLPM separates within-person dynamics from stable between-person traits). The within-person path from party to the later belief is more than triple the reverse path, and the difference is significant by bootstrap."
rd("voter_riclpm.csv") |>
  kable(col.names = c("Parameter", "Estimate", "SE", "p", "Note"))
```

The complementary descriptive trajectory (@fig-voter) and the sorting summary — party–belief alignment rising from 74% to 83%, with two-thirds of the 2011-misaligned converging by 2020 — together with the two-wave CLPM and change-score robustness are written by `R/17_voter_panel.R` to `voter_within_person_gap.csv`, `voter_cross_lagged.csv`, `voter_riclpm.csv`, and `voter_sorting.csv`. The RI-CLPM is reproducible in R via `lavaan` (model syntax in `R/17_voter_panel.R`); the committed `voter_riclpm.csv` records the estimates this manuscript renders.

# Appendix C — Reproducibility

The analysis is fully scripted and version-pinned. From the repository root, `source("setup.R")` restores the package versions recorded in `renv.lock`; `Rscript run_all.R` then runs `R/01`–`R/16` followed by the figure script, writing derived aggregates to `data/processed/`. A fixed seed (`20260616`) is set in `run_all.R`. This manuscript renders its tables and figures directly from the committed aggregates in `data/processed/`, so the document and the analysis cannot diverge; the aggregates are non-identifiable, allowing every exhibit to be rebuilt without the restricted microdata. All estimation was performed in R 4.6.0; design-based inference uses the `survey` package [@lumley2004analysis], with `tidyverse` for data manipulation and `haven` for survey-file import. Exact package versions are pinned in `renv.lock`; the public repository (with the commit hash recorded in the released version) holds the scripts, the lockfile, the committed aggregates, and this manuscript source. A clean run reproduces the following.

| Script | Object | Expected value |
|----|----|----|
| 01 | cleaned expert panel | 753 economist × sub-question rows |
| 02 | public–expert gap; micro model | AI gap +0.45; college OR 0.82 |
| 03 | Claim Verifiability Index | range 5–12, mean 9.5; Krippendorff's α = 0.88 |
| 04 | public–expert gaps | AI +0.45, trade +0.36, immigration +0.39 |
| 05 | tribalization gradient | party OR 1.04 → 1.70 → 3.79 |
| 06 | composition control | party×era OR 3.38; education×era null |
| 07 | precedence | lag-10 r = 0.92; Granger β = 0.72, p = .063 |
| 08 | partisanization (capstone) | gap −0.03 → +0.33; trend r = .92, p = .03 |
| 09 | mechanism (GSS) | gap emerges among graduates; 98% Democratic convergence |
| 10 | mechanism (ANES) | party×knowledge +0.51, p \< .001 |
| 11 | robustness | multiverse 100%/100%; knowledge survives education+ideology controls |
| 12 | convergence + behavior | fact gap 9% → 72% of preference; fact predicts vote (OR 7.6) |
| 13 | conditional law + descriptives | amplification: immigration + / automation null / AI − |

# Appendix D — Measurement: variables, coding, and question wording

## D.1 Matched pairs and question wording

Each folk claim pairs a public-opinion item with the economic experts' verdict on the same causal claim, framed so that public and expert agreement point the same way. The pairs are *conceptual* matches, not identical wordings: the expert items use precise technical language and the public items are deliberately broad. The AI pair is the closest — a belief about the same outcome on both sides — while the trade and immigration pairs match the public folk belief to the experts' verdict on a closely related policy-causal claim. We treat the trade and immigration pairs as illustrative context and place the inferential weight on the individual-level and over-time analyses of the public items themselves. Verbatim wordings:

| Pair | Expert claim (IGM / Kent A. Clark Center, verbatim) | Public item |
|----|----|----|
| AI → jobs | "Use of artificial intelligence over the next ten years will lead to a substantial increase in the unemployment rates in advanced countries." | Pew W152 `AIJOBS_W152`: "Thinking about the U.S. over the next 20 years, do you think that artificial intelligence (AI) will lead to \[more / fewer / about the same number of\] jobs?" (folk = "fewer") |
| Trade → jobs | "If all of the 'Seven actions to protect American workers' in President-elect Trump's 100-day plan are enacted, it will more likely than not improve the economic prospects of middle-class Americans over the next decade." | GSS `moretrde`: "(More) international trade leads to fewer jobs in the USA" (folk = agree) |
| Immigration → jobs | "Requiring most green card applicants to apply for permanent residency from overseas would lead to a substantial reduction in the numbers of skilled immigrants in the US." | GSS `immjobs`: "Immigrants take jobs away from people born in America" (folk = agree); ANES `V242228` (see D.3) |

The immigration benchmark is the most indirect of the three and warrants an explicit caveat. No IGM/Kent A. Clark Center item asks economists the verbatim folk claim, so we take the expert benchmark as the complement of the panel's near-unanimous agreement (97 percent) that curtailing green cards would *reduce* the number of skilled immigrants — a verdict that treats immigrants, including the highly skilled, as an economic asset rather than a cost. The implied share endorsing the folk premise that immigrants take jobs is its complement, roughly three percent, which aligns with the National Academies' consensus that immigration does not reduce native employment on net [@nas2017immigration]. We are explicit that this inversion is an approximation carrying no inferential weight: the paper's claims about immigration rest entirely on the over-time and individual-level analyses of the public `immjobs` item, not on the constructed benchmark.

## D.2 Variable coding

| Survey | Variable | Item label | Coding |
|----|----|----|----|
| GSS | `immjobs` | immigrants take jobs away (5-pt agree–disagree) | folk = 1 if (strongly) agree (≤ 2) |
| GSS | `letin1` | number of immigrants should be (5-pt) | restrictionist = 1 if reduce (≥ 4) |
| GSS | `letin1a` | number of immigrants nowadays should be (5-pt) | restrictionist = 1 if reduce (≥ 4) |
| GSS | `moretrde` | more trade, fewer US jobs | folk = 1 if agree (≤ 2) |
| GSS | `partyid` | political party affiliation (0–7) | Democrat ≤ 2, Republican ≥ 4 |
| GSS | `degree` | highest degree (0–4) | college = 1 if bachelor+ (≥ 3) |
| GSS | `wtssall` / `wtssps` | person (post-stratification) weight | analysis weight |
| Pew W152 | `AIJOBS_W152` | AI → more / fewer / same jobs | folk = 1 if "fewer" |
| Pew W27 | `ROBJOB4B_W27` | automation → people struggle to fill their time | folk = 1 if "likely" |
| Pew | `F_PARTYSUM_FINAL` | party summary | Republican vs Democrat |
| Pew | `F_EDUCCAT` / `F_EDUCCAT_FINAL` | education category | college = 1 if highest category |
| ANES | `V242228` | immigration likely to take jobs (4-pt) | fact = 1 if extremely/very likely |
| ANES | `V241227x` | party ID summary (1–7) | Democrat 1–3, Republican 5–7 |

## D.3 ANES 2024 knowledge battery

The dependent variable for the cross-survey mechanism test is `V242228` (post-election): "How likely is it that recent immigration levels will take jobs away from people already here?", coded 1 if "extremely" or "very" likely, 0 if "somewhat" or "not at all" likely. The political-knowledge index sums four items, each scored correct = 1:

| Variable | Item | Correct answer |
|----|----|----|
| `V241612` | Years in a full U.S. Senate term | 6 |
| `V241613` | Category of least federal spending | foreign aid |
| `V241614` | Party with most House members before the 2024 election | Republicans |
| `V241615` | Party with most Senate members before the 2024 election | Democrats |

The two majority items are scored to the **pre-November-2024 Congress** (Republican House, Democratic Senate). Estimation uses the post-election design: weight `V240107b`, primary sampling unit `V240107c`, stratum `V240107d`. ANES includes a "catch" knowledge item, and some respondents may look answers up; both work *against* detecting a knowledge effect, so neither threatens the positive interaction reported.

# Appendix E — Pre-registered future experiment

The cleanest test of the mechanism — and the decisive adjudication of sincere identity-protective cognition versus expressive responding [@bullock2015partisan; @prior2015serious] — is experimental, and is deferred here for IRB and affiliation reasons rather than as an oversight. The planned design has three arms: (i) a **de-tribalization** arm presenting the expert consensus either stripped of partisan cues or delivered by a co-partisan ("trusted in-group messenger") source; (ii) a **mechanism-explanation** arm following @meyers2020inducing; and (iii) an **incentivized-accuracy** arm following @prior2015serious, paying for correct answers to partition the gap into sincere and expressive components. It tests three hypotheses, each mapped to an arm: **H1 (de-tribalization)** — removing partisan cues, or sourcing the consensus from a co-partisan, narrows the out-group's gap on the fact; **H2 (mechanism vs. information)** — eliciting a causal explanation moves belief toward the experts more on uncontested than on contested claims; **H3 (sincerity)** — accuracy incentives reduce but do not eliminate the partisan gap. Anticipating a treatment effect of 8–12 percentage points on the gap, roughly 500 respondents per cell (≈ 2,000 total) yields 80% power at $\alpha = .05$; the pre-registration will fix the analysis plan, covariates, and exclusion rules before data collection. The predictions follow directly from the two-regime model: information and mechanism explanation move belief in the folk regime, whereas only de-tribalization or a trusted in-group source moves it in the identity regime. Separately, the model's *forward* prediction — that AI-and-employment beliefs, weakly sorted in 2024, will partisanize as the issue tribalizes — is registered prospectively (`paper/preregistration.md`), so that the next fact to sort tests the theory in advance rather than in hindsight.
